coach_says: d3 is a sound move: it stops ...e4 from hitting your pinned knight on f3 and opens the road for your c1 bishop. h3 was slightly cleaner, asking the g4 bishop straight away whether it wants to trade on f3, but there is nothing here a player needs to fix.
also: put the question to the pinning bishop with h3

coach_says: Taking the bishop was the only good move, and you found it. Kf8 would have lost on the spot to Qd8+ Kxf7 Ng5 mate. You are a piece up now; finish developing and keep your king tucked away.

You are two pawns down in a rook endgame and nearly every move leads to the same difficult result. c4 is as good as the alternatives; the practical task is to keep your king active and make Black's rook work to win your pawns.

Your queen on b5 was attacked by the d5 rook, and Rc7+ deals with it by checking first, so Black has to block with the bishop before you move the queen. That is a perfectly good way to handle it; Qa4, moving the queen while it hits a7, was just as strong.
also: check before you move the attacked piece

coach_says: Bc4 is playable, but against the Sicilian the bishop aims at f7 and Black can block it with ...e6 and then hit it with ...d5, gaining time. Nf3 keeps more options and prepares d4. It is a small difference, but worth knowing which openings this bishop move suits.
a6 is a fine move: it asks the b5 bishop to decide now. If White takes on c6 you get the bishop pair for slightly weaker pawns, which is a fair trade. Developing with Be7 or Nf6 was just as good.

You are already a queen for a bishop down here, so the game is very hard whatever you play. Nd4 saves the knight from ...gxf5, but it lets Black check on h4 and keep your king in the middle; checking with Ng7+ first was slightly more stubborn. Nothing here changes the result.
Rh2 is a good plan: you are preparing to double rooks on the h-file and go after the h5 pawn. The engine likes rerouting the a4 knight with Nb2 first, but your move is just as strong in practice.
also: double rooks on the open file

coach_says: Your e7 bishop was attacked by the queen, and Bb4 saves it while hitting the queen, but White just plays a3 and the bishop has to move again, so White gains a free move. Nc6 protects e7 and brings a new piece into the game at the same time. When you are ahead in material, finish developing; one-move attacks that get kicked away just give the opponent time.

When the a4 knight attacked your b6 bishop, you defended it with Qc7, which is passive. Nd4 was much stronger: the knight hits the queen on b5, the f3 knight and c2, and if White grabs Nxb6 you play Nxb5 and win the queen. When a piece of yours is attacked, first look for a counterattack that gains time.

Before b5 you needed to see Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+: the knight check moves off the d1-g4 diagonal and the queen takes your undefended bishop on g4. b5 attacks the c4 bishop but White simply plays the trick first. Nf6 develops and guards g4 at the same time; whenever you have a bishop on g4 with nothing protecting it, check for discovered attacks on it.
also: missed the Bxf7+ and Ng5+ threat

coach_says: Your rook on e6 was attacked by the f4 knight and needed the f7 pawn to recapture. After f5 that pawn has gone, so Nxe6+ comes with check and you can only recapture with the knight, losing the exchange; then exf5 gxf5 Bxf5 pins your e6 knight to the c8 rook. Before pushing a pawn, ask what it was protecting. Rce8, doubling behind the rook, kept everything defended.

You had to stop Nc7+, which forks your king and the a8 rook, and Kd8 does that by covering c7, but it leaves your king in the middle and boxes in your queenside. Rb8 moves the rook off the fork square and keeps the king free; Black then plays ...d6 and develops normally. Against a fork, moving the target is often better than putting your king on guard duty.

Your g4 knight was attacked by the f3 pawn, but retreating to h6 opened the g-file: Rg6 attacks your queen, and the queen cannot take because the g2 queen guards g6. Worse, your g7 pawn is pinned to your king, so it cannot defend h6, and you lose heavy material. Instead Rxd4 counterattacked: after cxd4 Qxd4+ your knight comes in with checks and wins the f4 bishop. Before you move a blocking piece, check which line it opens to your king.
concept: opened the g-file to your king

coach_says: The g7 knight was free: both your g5 and f7 rooks attacked it and only the f6 pawn defended it. Rgxg7 wins it, because if fxg7 then Rxf1 is mate on the back rank. Take with the g5 rook, not the f7 one, so the f-file opens onto White's king. Rg6 let the knight escape and the advantage vanished.

Kg2 walks into a knight fork: Ne1+ checks your king and attacks the c2 bishop at the same time, and you lose the bishop. Kf1 or Kh1 avoids the e1 square trick and keeps you better. In endgames with knights on the board, look at every check the knight has before you move your king.

f6 kicks the g5 bishop, but sends it straight to c1 where it attacks your a3 bishop. That bishop is stuck, because it is pinned by the a1 rook to your queen on a8, so you lose it (White can even check on e6 first). Better was Nxg5 to remove the bishop, or Qb7 to unpin. Before chasing a piece, ask where it wants to go.
also: chased the bishop to a better square

coach_says: White's king sits on c2 and White is about to storm your king with h4 and g5. Qe8 does nothing about that, and it also stops your queen guarding h4, so ...Bxh4 is no longer possible. c6 was the right reaction: hit the d5 pawn and open lines towards White's king. When the kings are on different wings, the race matters, so use every move to attack, not to wait.

Be7 retreats into a passive spot and lets White play Be6+ and Bd7, harassing your e8 knight. White's king on h1 has no defenders, so Qc5 was better: the queen centralises and threatens checks on c1 and e3. In queen endings, an active queen and checks against a loose king usually matter more than tidying up your bishop.

White threatened Qh7 mate: the queen lands on h7 protected by the g6 pawn, and your king has no square because the g6 pawn also covers f7. Qc5 ignores it. Nf5 blocks the threat by attacking the h6 queen. When your opponent's queen and pawn are this close to your king, check their mating moves before you start your own plans.
